title: Protein quality: what do PDCAAS and DIAAS mean?

seo.title: PDCAAS vs. DIAAS: how protein quality is measured
seo.meta_description: PDCAAS and DIAAS both combine essential amino acids and digestibility, but differently. Learn what each score means, its limits and how to interpret it.
seo.search_intent: Understand PDCAAS and DIAAS, how each evaluates protein quality, and what a protein-quality score can and cannot tell you.

excerpt: PDCAAS and DIAAS ask a similar question: how well a protein supplies essential amino acids after accounting for digestion. PDCAAS combines the limiting-amino-acid score with overall fecal protein digestibility and commonly truncates scores at 1.00; DIAAS uses ileal digestibility for each indispensable amino acid and does not need to truncate values above 100. FAO recommends DIAAS as the more informative method, while PDCAAS remains relevant in U.S. protein-label calculations.
content_html:
A label saying 20 g of protein tells you how much protein is present, not how its essential amino acids line up with human needs or how well those amino acids are digested. PDCAAS and DIAAS are attempts to add that missing dimension.

PDCAAS combines a limiting amino acid with overall digestibility

PDCAAS stands for Protein Digestibility-Corrected Amino Acid Score. It first compares the most limiting essential amino acid in a protein with a human requirement pattern, then adjusts the score using an estimate of overall protein digestibility.

The classic method uses fecal nitrogen digestibility, measured after material has passed through the large intestine as well as the small intestine. Results are usually expressed from 0 to 1.00, with higher calculated values truncated to 1.00.

Truncation hides differences above the reference target

Imagine two proteins with untruncated calculated scores of 1.05 and 1.25. Under a 1.00 cap, they both appear as 1.00 versus 1.00. The score no longer shows that one provides a larger surplus of digestible indispensable amino acids relative to the reference pattern.

That may be adequate for asking whether a protein meets a threshold, but it loses information when comparing ingredients or designing complementary protein mixtures.

DIAAS measures each amino acid before the colon

DIAAS stands for Digestible Indispensable Amino Acid Score. Instead of applying one digestibility number to the whole protein, it estimates ileal digestibility for each indispensable amino acid—how much has disappeared by the end of the small intestine, before colonic microbes can alter nitrogen compounds.

The digestible amount of each amino acid is compared with an age-appropriate reference pattern, and the lowest ratio determines DIAAS. Scores can remain above 100, preserving information that PDCAAS truncation can hide.

Why FAO recommended DIAAS

FAO's 2013 expert consultation recommended DIAAS as the preferred method because it treats amino acids individually, uses ileal rather than fecal digestibility, and addresses several recognized PDCAAS limitations.

Adoption is not instantaneous. Ileal digestibility data are more difficult and expensive to generate for many foods, and regulatory systems do not change at the same pace as scientific recommendations. In the United States, PDCAAS remains embedded in how corrected protein amounts can be calculated for certain Nutrition Facts labeling situations.

A high protein score is not a total-health score

PDCAAS and DIAAS evaluate protein quality. They do not directly score fiber, sodium, saturated fat, omega-3 fats, vitamins, minerals, processing, price, or environmental impact.

A bean protein can score below a dairy protein because of a limiting amino acid and lower digestibility, while the beans provide fiber that an isolated dairy protein does not. That is not a contradiction; the two scores are answering different questions.

A mixed diet can outperform the score of one ingredient

Foods are eaten together. A protein relatively low in lysine can be complemented by another food that supplies more lysine, improving the amino-acid balance of the mixture. One ingredient's score therefore does not predict the quality of an entire varied diet.

When you see a protein-quality number, ask three things: which method was used, which age reference pattern was used, and whether the value describes a whole food or a purified protein ingredient. With that context, PDCAAS and DIAAS are useful tools rather than mysterious grades.

faq.question: What does PDCAAS stand for?
faq.answer: Protein Digestibility-Corrected Amino Acid Score. It compares the limiting essential amino acid with a reference pattern and adjusts for overall protein digestibility.

faq.question: How is DIAAS different?
faq.answer: DIAAS uses ileal digestibility for each indispensable amino acid separately and retains scores above 100, giving more resolution.

faq.question: Does a higher DIAAS mean the whole food is healthier?
faq.answer: No. DIAAS evaluates protein quality, not fiber, fat quality, sodium, micronutrients, processing, or the overall health value of a food.
